Stage 02

Statutory Formation & Board Resolutions

Competent registry, governing statute, capital lockup rules, and first board resolution template.

Competent corporate registry

Registro Mercantil Provincial (Provincial Mercantile Registry) of the province where the registered office is established; name reservation is processed through the Registro Mercantil Central.

Governing statute

Royal Legislative Decree 1/2010, of 2 July, approving the consolidated text of the Ley de Sociedades de Capital (Spanish Companies Act), notably Articles 20, 22, 23, 58-62 and 210 (registered office, share capital, deed of incorporation, administrative body).

Formation / constitutional filings

Escritura de Constitución (public deed of incorporation) executed before a Spanish notary and thereafter registered in the Mercantile Registry.

Incorporation processing time

⚡ 38 business days (SOP sum)

Paid-up Capital & Blocked Account Regime No Capital Lockup Account Required

The SL must have a minimum share capital of EUR 3,000, fully subscribed and fully paid at incorporation; cash contributions must be evidenced by a Spanish bank deposit certificate or notary deposit; no escrow account is required under Spanish law.

Funding & unlock path: Fire safety certification (certificado de protección contra incendios) and approved fire-fighting installations are required before opening; structural load inspection of the storage racking system must be certified; occupational risk prevention assessment (Riesgos Laborales) and the company's adherence to workplace safety rules under Ley 31/1995 are mandatory for employees.

Paid-in capital rule: The SL must have a minimum share capital of EUR 3,000, fully subscribed and fully paid at incorporation; cash contributions must be evidenced by a Spanish bank deposit certificate or notary deposit; no escrow account is required under Spanish law.

Pro-Forma First Board Resolution Draft
RESOLVED: (1) The founder hereby subscribes and fully pays the entire share capital of EUR 3,000, divided into 3,000 indivisible participations of EUR 1 each, and approves the articles of association as set forth in the public deed; (2) The registered office shall be established at [Address], Spain, and the administrative body is authorized to open bank accounts and to take all steps needed to obtain the tax identification number, register the company in the Mercantile Registry, and secure municipal operating licenses; (3) [Name and ID] is appointed sole administrator with all statutory powers, including representation before public and private bodies.
Industrial Access / EIA & Civil Defense Approval Mandatory Environmental Clearance

Municipal Licensing Authority (Ayuntamiento) – generally the Concejalía de Urbanismo, Actividades y Licencias of the municipality where the warehouse and packaging premises are located.

Category: Licencia Municipal de Actividad y Apertura (or Declaración Responsable de Apertura) for the operation of a warehouse and subscription-box packaging facility.

Stage 03

Tax Identity & Indirect Tax

Tax authority e-portal, entity tax classification elections, VAT thresholds, and 0% export documentation chain.

Tax ID Application Infrastructure

Competent tax authority

Agencia Estatal de Administración Tributaria (AEAT), including the Sede Electrónica de la Agencia Tributaria. The AEAT administers the Spanish Tax Identification Number (NIF), Value Added Tax (VAT), Intrastat, and related national tax registrations.

E-government filing portal

A Spanish Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada obtains a provisional NIF from the AEAT, generally through Modelo 036, using the incorporation deed, articles of association, evidence of registered office, identification of directors and representatives, and duly legalized or apostilled and translated documents for foreign parties where applicable. Following registration of the deed with the competent Registro Mercantil, the company files the required information with the AEAT to obtain or confirm its definitive NIF. The Spanish NIF normally also serves as the domestic VAT identification number. An entity carrying out intra-Community acquisitions or supplies applies through Modelo 036 for registration in the Registro de Operadores Intracomunitarios (ROI); the resulting VAT number is the NIF prefixed by 'ES' and is activated for VIES purposes after AEAT validation. A foreign entity without a Spanish establishment may obtain an NIF through Modelo 036, directly or through an authorized representative. Non-EU businesses conducting Spanish VAT activities may generally be required to appoint a Spanish VAT representative, subject to applicable statutory exceptions and international arrangements. VAT registration must be completed before the relevant taxable activities commence.

Tax ID type & application path: Entity_Level_Taxation — A Spanish Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada obtains a provisional NIF from the AEAT, generally through Modelo 036, using the incorporation deed, articles of association, evidence of registered office, identification of directors and representatives, and duly legalized or apostilled and translated documents for foreign parties where applicable. Following registration of the deed with the competent Registro Mercantil, the company files the required information with the AEAT to obtain or confirm its definitive NIF. The Spanish NIF normally also serves as the domestic VAT identification number. An entity carrying out intra-Community acquisitions or supplies applies through Modelo 036 for registration in the Registro de Operadores Intracomunitarios (ROI); the resulting VAT number is the NIF prefixed by 'ES' and is activated for VIES purposes after AEAT validation. A foreign entity without a Spanish establishment may obtain an NIF through Modelo 036, directly or through an authorized representative. Non-EU businesses conducting Spanish VAT activities may generally be required to appoint a Spanish VAT representative, subject to applicable statutory exceptions and international arrangements. VAT registration must be completed before the relevant taxable activities commence.

Default Tax Classification & Elections

Default tax classification

Entity_Level_Taxation

Available election forms

There is no Spanish equivalent of a general United States check-the-box election for an SL. A Spanish SL is ordinarily subject to Spanish Corporate Income Tax as a separate legal person. Specific statutory regimes may be elected or applied if their conditions are met, including consolidated tax grouping, the special regime for entities in the Canary Islands where applicable, and other sector-specific regimes. Spanish and EU anti-hybrid mismatch rules implement ATAD measures and can deny deductions, tax exempt income, or impose inclusion consequences; they do not provide a general elective hybrid classification. A Spanish SL may also access VAT special regimes relevant to its activities, including the One-Stop Shop regimes for qualifying cross-border consumer supplies.

VAT / GST & 0% Export Zero-Rating

Standard VAT / GST rate

21%

Mandatory registration threshold (Nexus)

No general domestic VAT turnover threshold applies in Spain. A person carrying out an independent economic activity must generally register before commencing taxable operations, irrespective of turnover. The EUR 10,000 EU-wide threshold is relevant to certain intra-EU business-to-consumer distance sales and electronically supplied, telecommunications, broadcasting, and electronic services, not to general Spanish domestic VAT registration. Qualifying EU consumer supplies may instead be reported through the Union OSS regime; qualifying imported consignments not exceeding EUR 150 may fall within IOSS.

Export 0% zero-rating conditions

Exports of goods from the Spanish VAT territory to destinations outside the European Union may qualify for exemption with the right to deduct, economically equivalent to zero-rating, under Article 21 of Law 37/1992, provided the goods leave the VAT territory and the supplier retains reliable evidence of export and transport. The export declaration and customs exit confirmation, normally evidenced through the MRN, exit results, or equivalent customs records, are central evidence. Intra-EU supplies of goods may qualify for exemption with the right to deduct under separate intra-Community supply rules when the customer has a valid VAT number in another Member State, the goods are transported to that Member State, and required recapitulative and documentary conditions are met. Services supplied to business customers established outside Spain are generally outside the scope of Spanish VAT under the place-of-supply rules, rather than technically zero-rated, subject to use-and-enjoyment rules and sector-specific exceptions. Consumer services require analysis of the applicable B2C place-of-supply rule. Export-related input VAT refunds require valid invoices, proof of taxable business activity, and compliance with the relevant periodic return or non-established-business refund procedure.

  • Customs export declaration containing the Movement Reference Number (MRN) or equivalent export reference
  • Electronic customs exit confirmation, exit results, or equivalent evidence that the goods left the EU customs and VAT territory
  • Commercial invoice identifying the supplier, customer, goods, value, and VAT treatment
  • Transport documentation, such as bill of lading, airway bill, CMR consignment note, courier record, or equivalent logistics evidence
  • Packing list and warehouse or carrier delivery records where necessary to reconcile the goods with the customs declaration
  • Proof of delivery or receipt by the non-EU customer where available
  • Payment records or other commercial evidence supporting the transaction and customer identity
  • For intra-Community supplies, the customer VAT identification number, transport evidence to another Member State, and required EC Sales List reporting

Spain does not operate a universal real-time pre-clearance system for all private-sector invoices. Businesses within the Immediate Supply of Information (SII) regime, including entities with annual turnover exceeding EUR 6 million, VAT groups, and REDEME-registered businesses, electronically submit prescribed VAT invoice-record data to the AEAT, generally within four business days, subject to statutory exceptions. Electronic invoicing is mandatory for transactions with Spanish public authorities under applicable public-procurement rules and uses required structured formats and platforms, including FACe where applicable. Law 18/2022 and its implementing framework establish phased private-sector B2B electronic-invoicing obligations, with detailed effective dates dependent on implementing regulations. Royal Decree 1007/2023 regulates compliant billing-record systems and the AEAT-facing requirements commonly referred to as VeriFactu, including integrity, traceability, preservation, and anti-tampering controls. A universal invoice-by-invoice digital stamp or real-time clearance requirement does not currently apply to every Spanish SL.

Spain has no general statutory foreign-exchange repatriation deadline for export proceeds and no general 180-day repatriation rule applicable to Spanish VAT zero-rating. Export exemption depends on the substantive export and evidence requirements, not on a mandatory repatriation period. If the export is not proven, the AEAT may reassess Spanish VAT, deny related input-tax recovery or refund claims, and charge statutory late-payment interest. Deliberate or negligent incorrect VAT treatment may trigger penalties under General Tax Law 58/2003, including penalties commonly calculated as a percentage of unpaid tax, with aggravated cases potentially reaching 100% to 150% of the amount improperly omitted, depending on the infringement and circumstances. Incorrect or fraudulent invoicing may generate separate invoicing penalties. False customs declarations may also result in customs debt, customs penalties, seizure or forfeiture measures, and potentially criminal liability for serious tax or customs fraud. Voluntary correction, complete transaction records, consistent customs data, and retention of evidence supporting exit, transport, customer identity, and accounting treatment are essential to reduce clawback exposure.

Stage 04

Banking & Treasury Architecture

Central-bank FX diagnosis, tier-1 local banks vs offshore digital EMI matrix, and KYC rejection defense guide.

Foreign Exchange Regime & Central Bank Policy

Current-account convertibility

The euro is fully convertible. Spain maintains complete liberalisation of capital and current account transactions under EU Treaty provisions (Articles 63-65 TFEU) and Royal Decree 1816/1991, as amended. Capital account transactions require ex-post statistical declarations to DGTOE for foreign direct investment where the participation reaches 10% or more or the value exceeds EUR 3,000,000; prior authorisation is not required. Profit remittance is unrestricted, but dividends paid by a Spanish SL to non-residents are subject to withholding tax under the Non-Resident Income Tax legislation (Royal Legislative Decree 5/2004) unless reduced by an applicable tax treaty or the EU Parent-Subsidiary Directive. No material exchange control hurdles exist for a subscription-box service operating through a Spanish SL.

Export proceeds surrender rules

Spain does not impose mandatory export proceeds surrender or forced conversion ratios. Under Royal Decree 1816/1991 and Banco de España Circular 4/2012, exporters must report collections from foreign sales for balance-of-payments statistical purposes if the transaction value exceeds EUR 12,500. Export receipts in foreign currency may be retained in authorised accounts or converted freely. No statutory conversion timeline applies. The exporter must submit the required declaration to Banco de España within the month following the transaction, retaining supporting commercial documentation for audit.

Central bank supervision: Banco de España (Bank of Spain) acting as the competent central banking and macroprudential authority; foreign exchange and investment control processing is delegated to the Dirección General de Transacciones y Operaciones Exteriores (DGTOE) of the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Business.

Offshore Digital Bank / EMI Whitelist

Cross-border EMI / Fintech rails Fit: High

High feasibility with legal constraints. An EU/EEA Electronic Money Institution (EMI) licensed under the Payment Services Directive (EU) 2015/2366 may passport into Spain and offer e-money accounts and payment services; however, it cannot fully substitute a Spanish resident bank account for all treasury functions, particularly for holding statutory corporate funds or for direct TARGET2 participation. Non-EU EMIs require a branch authorisation or must operate through a registered Spanish payment institution. For a Spanish SL, the recommended structure is a tier-1 Spanish bank account supplemented by a fintech EMI for high-speed cross-border disbursements and multicurrency float, subject to bank-approved remittance routing and client-money segregation rules.

Core KYC Rejection Triggers & Defense Dossier

Beneficial ownership chain involving high-risk or non-cooperative jurisdictions

Root cause: Beneficial ownership chain involving high-risk or non-cooperative jurisdictions

Defense evidence: Extract from the Registro de Titularidades Reales (Spanish beneficial ownership register); certified shareholding structure; notarised passports and proof of physical directors; CRS tax residence declarations; evidence of real economic activity in Spain including local payroll, leased warehouse, and supplier contracts.
Large expected inbound capital injection to the escrow account

Root cause: Large expected inbound capital injection to the escrow account

Defense evidence: Executed capital increase deed formalised before a Spanish notary and registered in the Registro Mercantil; board/shareholder resolution authorising the capital contribution; bank reference letter from the remitting institution; source of wealth statement for non-resident investors; intermediary payment chain disclosure and transfer purpose documentation.
Anticipated cross-border payout concentration to merchants or logistics providers in sanction-list exposed regions

Root cause: Anticipated cross-border payout concentration to merchants or logistics providers in sanction-list exposed regions

Defense evidence: EU restrictive measures and OFAC screening certificates for all counterparties; transaction-level commercial invoices and contracts; shipping and logistics documentation including CN22 or airway bills and customs declarations; e-commerce marketplace agreements; annual AML compliance certification proving continuous monitoring.
Mismatch between declared ISIC 4791 activity and corporate financial flows

Root cause: Mismatch between declared ISIC 4791 activity and corporate financial flows

Defense evidence: Certified tax residency certificate; Spanish tax filings (Modelo 200 and Modelo 390); IAE census extract; detailed subscription-box business plan with revenue recognition policy; host-to-country intercompany agreements showing commercial substance.

Cross-Border Clearing Corridors & Settlement Fit

Inbound equity or shareholder-loan funding must be remitted via SWIFT MT103 from the investor's bank to the SL's euro-denominated account in Spain. The wire should contain the EU/FDI purpose code for foreign direct investment, with full remittance information in field 70, referencing the underlying investment declaration. Where the investment exceeds EUR 3,000,000 or the participation threshold is reached after the operation, the SL must file the online DGTOE foreign direct investment declaration within one month of formalisation. Verification is performed by the receiving bank through sanctions screening, beneficial ownership matching, and confirmation that the inbound credit matches the filed investment structure. Sterling, US-dollar and Latin American currency cables may be accepted through correspondent banks and converted into EUR on arrival, always respecting the declared purpose and FX compliance checks.Outbound supplier, logistics and marketing payments should be executed through SWIFT MT103 customer credit transfers using SEPA rails for euro-denominated domestic settlements and correspondent banking for non-EU trade creditors. For larger subscription-box merchandise procurements, commercial letters of credit under ICC UCP600 are permissible; presentation documents must comply with ISBP 745 to avoid discrepancies. The remittance field 70 must contain the applicable trade in goods or services purpose code and reference the underlying commercial invoice. Parties should use TARGET2 settlement for intraday euro flows and leverage Spanish banking APIs for automatic reconciliation. For Latin American vendor payouts, prudent treasury practice uses segregated multicurrency accounts held in the Spanish bank or through an EMI partner, with NDF execution as required for currencies lacking onshore deliverability.FX forward contracts (deliverable EUR/USD and EUR/LATAM currency forwards) up to 12-month tenorNon-deliverable forwards (NDFs) for restricted Latin American currencies where onshore FX conversion is unavailable or non-tradeableFX swap and rollover contracts for short-term cross-currency liquidity managementCross-currency interest rate swaps for medium-term balance-sheet hedging of funding liabilities

E-commerce / gateway settlement fit: High feasibility with legal constraints. An EU/EEA Electronic Money Institution (EMI) licensed under the Payment Services Directive (EU) 2015/2366 may passport into Spain and offer e-money accounts and payment services; however, it cannot fully substitute a Spanish resident bank account for all treasury functions, particularly for holding statutory corporate funds or for direct TARGET2 participation. Non-EU EMIs require a branch authorisation or must operate through a registered Spanish payment institution. For a Spanish SL, the recommended structure is a tier-1 Spanish bank account supplemented by a fintech EMI for high-speed cross-border disbursements and multicurrency float, subject to bank-approved remittance routing and client-money segregation rules.

Stage 05

Annual Statutory Maintenance

Statutory filing calendar, progressive late penalties, external audit triggers, and statutory registers.

Statutory Filing Calendar

Statutory deliverableDeadline window Government feeDelinquency sanctions
Approval and filing of annual accounts (Cuentas Anuales) with the Mercantile Registry The shareholders' meeting must approve the annual accounts within six months of the financial year-end; the approved accounts must be filed with the Mercantile Registry within one month after approval. For a calendar-year SL, approval is due no later than 30 June and deposit is commonly due no later than 30 July. $13 USD Late deposit triggers closure of the company's corporate file (cierre registral), preventing the registration of subsequent corporate deeds; non-deposit for two consecutive financial years causes the Mercantile Registry to close the registration sheet. There is no automatic administrative strike-off, but prolonged closure blocks all public filings and may lead to judicial dissolution at the request of the tax authority or affected parties; directors may incur liability for continued non-compliance.
Corporate income tax annual return (Modelo 200) Due within 25 days after the six-month period following the end of the tax period; for a calendar-year entity, no later than 25 July of the following year. $0 USD Late filing or payment triggers late-filing surcharges of 5%, 10%, 15% or 20% depending on the delay, plus late-payment interest. AEAT may assess the tax using partial or estimated data. Persistent non-filing and non-payment can lead to enforcement of assessed liabilities, director liability, and forfeiture of tax benefits; it does not by itself trigger administrative strike-off under mercantile law.
Annual third-party transactions information return (Modelo 347), if any supplier or customer transactions exceed EUR 3,005.06 in the calendar year Filing opens on 1 February and closes on 28 February (or 29 February in a leap year) for the preceding calendar year. $0 USD Late, inaccurate or incomplete submissions are subject to penalties under the General Tax Law, with a minimum penalty of EUR 300 for incorrect data and penalties that can reach 75% of the relevant amounts, plus late-payment interest. Administrative strike-off is not a direct tax consequence, but continued non-compliance intensifies tax enforcement actions against the entity and directors.
Electronic legalization of statutory accounting books (Libro Diario and Libro de Inventarios y Cuentas Anuales) Within four months after the end of the financial year; for calendar-year books, submission for legalization must be completed no later than 30 April of the following year. $13 USD Unlegalized books have reduced evidentiary value in commercial proceedings and may be rejected for certain corporate filings; record-keeping failures can be penalized by the tax administration under the General Tax Law. The registry does not administratively strike off the company for this default, but the defect may impair annual accounts deposit and contribute to registry closure.
Annual return deadline

The shareholders' meeting must approve the annual accounts within six months of the financial year-end; the approved accounts must be filed with the Mercantile Registry within one month after approval. For a calendar-year SL, approval is due no later than 30 June and deposit is commonly due no later than 30 July.

Statutory government annual fee

$13 USD

Late filing penalties

Late deposit triggers closure of the company's corporate file (cierre registral), preventing the registration of subsequent corporate deeds; non-deposit for two consecutive financial years causes the Mercantile Registry to close the registration sheet. There is no automatic administrative strike-off, but prolonged closure blocks all public filings and may lead to judicial dissolution at the request of the tax authority or affected parties; directors may incur liability for continued non-compliance.

Strike-off trigger

Mandatory Audit Threshold Small Company Audit Exemption Regime

Turnover: An independent registered auditor is required when, for two consecutive financial years, the SL meets at least two of the following criteria: total assets exceed EUR 2,850,000; annual net turnover exceeds EUR 5,700,000; average annual number of employees exceeds 50. An audit may also be required by shareholders representing at least 5% of the share capital, by sector-specific rules, or by the terms of financing agreements.

Stage 06

Corporate Tax & Transfer Pricing

Corporate income tax (CIT), box-by-box return breakdown, dividend WHT, and director personal liability.

Statutory corporate income tax (CIT)

25% general Spanish corporate income tax rate. Qualifying newly created entities generally apply 15% in the first tax period in which they obtain a positive taxable base and the following tax period, subject to statutory exclusions. Qualifying start-up companies may apply 15% during the period in which start-up status is obtained and the following three tax periods, subject to conditions. Special reduced rates for micro-enterprises and small entities are subject to turnover thresholds and phased statutory changes; confirm the rate for the relevant tax year.

Dividend withholding tax (WHT)

19% Spanish domestic withholding on dividends paid to non-residents, subject to exemptions and treaty relief. A qualifying EU parent may obtain exemption under the Parent-Subsidiary Directive as implemented in Spain, generally requiring a qualifying holding (normally at least 5%, or the statutory acquisition-cost alternative), minimum holding period, eligible form and tax status, and anti-abuse compliance. Treaty rates vary by recipient jurisdiction and beneficial ownership.

Mandatory Return Breakdown

Deadline: · Frequency:

Modelo 200: Within 25 calendar days following the six months after the end of the tax period. For a calendar-year taxpayer, the usual deadline is 25 July. Modelo 202: Generally 1–20 April, October, and December; the precise deadline and payment calculation depend on the applicable statutory method and calendar.

Deadline: · Frequency:

Generally 1–20 April, October, and December, subject to the official calendar and applicable calculation method.

Transfer Pricing & Economic Substance

Master / Local File threshold: Spanish related-party transactions must generally be valued at arm's length and documented. The full documentation obligation is generally relieved for transactions with the same related party whose aggregate consideration does not exceed EUR 250,000 in the tax period, subject to statutory exceptions. Simplified documentation may apply to entities or groups with net turnover below EUR 45 million, subject to exclusions. Master File requirements generally apply to groups with consolidated net turnover of at least EUR 45 million. Additional country-by-country reporting generally applies to qualifying multinational groups with consolidated revenue of at least EUR 750 million.

Economic substance scope: Spain has no general UAE-style Economic Substance Regulations regime. Spanish transfer-pricing, beneficial-ownership, anti-abuse, controlled-foreign-company, permanent-establishment, and tax-residence rules may nevertheless challenge arrangements lacking commercial rationale, personnel, decision-making, or functions consistent with reported income. A Spanish SL should maintain evidence of its actual management, operations, contractual functions, assets, and risks.

Fatal Compliance Red Lines & Director Liability

Corporate tax evasion and fraudulent returns

Statutory sanction: Administrative penalties generally range from 50% to 150% of the tax shortfall, depending on the infringement and aggravating circumstances, in addition to tax and interest. Tax fraud may constitute a criminal offence where the amount defrauded exceeds EUR 120,000 per tax and tax period; the basic criminal penalty may include imprisonment of one to five years and a fine of one to six times the defrauded amount. Aggravated cases may carry higher penalties.

Director personal liability: Directors may face criminal liability where they personally participate in or authorise fraud, and may incur civil or tax liability under statutory conditions for their own conduct or failure to perform legal duties. Imprisonment and ancillary disqualifications may apply following criminal conviction. Travel restrictions are not an automatic tax penalty.
Transfer-pricing non-compliance

Statutory sanction: The AEAT may adjust taxable income and assess tax and interest. Specific documentation and reporting failures may attract fixed penalties, including amounts calculated per missing or incorrect data item, subject to statutory caps; an adjustment without a qualifying tax shortfall may also trigger a penalty calculated by reference to the adjustment. Exact exposure depends on the infringement, documentation, and tax result.

Director personal liability: Directors are not automatically personally liable for the SL's transfer-pricing tax debt. Liability may arise under statutory derivation rules for culpable participation, obstruction, or breach of duties, and criminal liability may apply where conduct forms part of tax fraud.
False invoicing and VAT fraud

Statutory sanction: VAT assessments, late-payment interest, and administrative penalties apply; serious or very serious infringements can carry substantial percentage-based fines. Conduct meeting the criminal tax-fraud threshold or constituting document fraud may also lead to criminal prosecution.

Director personal liability: Personal criminal or derivative liability may apply where a director knowingly directs, facilitates, or conceals the conduct. The SL's limited-liability form does not protect a director from liability for personal wrongdoing.
Undeclared payroll, social security, or worker misclassification

Statutory sanction: Back taxes, social-security contributions, surcharges, interest, and administrative fines may apply. Serious cases can result in criminal liability under applicable Spanish tax, social-security, or labour offences.

Director personal liability: Directors may be personally liable where statutory requirements for derivative liability or criminal participation are met. Imprisonment is possible for qualifying criminal conduct; it is not an automatic consequence of an administrative assessment.
Money laundering and suspicious payment flows

Statutory sanction: Money-laundering offences may result in imprisonment, fines, confiscation, and ancillary measures under Spanish criminal law. Administrative AML sanctions depend on whether the business is an obliged entity and on the breach; ordinary retail subscription activity does not by itself make the SL an AML-obliged entity.

Director personal liability: Directors and managers may face personal criminal liability for knowing participation, concealment, or serious supervisory failures where the legal elements are met. Corporate criminal liability may also arise for qualifying offences committed for the company's benefit.
Abusive shell or conduit structure

Statutory sanction: The AEAT may deny treaty or domestic-law benefits, recharacterise transactions, adjust taxable income, and assess tax, interest, and applicable penalties. Criminal consequences require conduct meeting the elements and thresholds of a criminal offence.

Director personal liability: Directors may face liability for deliberate fraud, false declarations, or culpable breach of statutory duties. Limited liability is not automatically disregarded merely because the company has limited operations or foreign shareholders.
Failure to maintain corporate and tax records

Statutory sanction: The tax authority may reject unsupported deductions or credits and impose statutory recordkeeping, reporting, or tax-return penalties, with tax, interest, and further penalties where an underpayment results.

Director personal liability: Directors may incur personal or derivative liability where their own conduct satisfies statutory conditions, including intentional destruction or concealment of records. A filing or recordkeeping breach alone does not automatically pierce the corporate veil.
